course.title: Healthcare
course.desc: Patient summaries, clinical notes, diagnosis support, treatment planning.

exercises.title: Vague vs. precise
exercises.sc:
A nurse practitioner needs to hand off a complex patient to the incoming shift. She types:

"Summarize this patient."

The AI returns a generic paragraph that misses the critical medication change from two hours ago and the pending lab results.
exercises.task: Write a better prompt. Be specific about: what clinical details matter (vitals, meds, pending orders), what format you want, and what to flag as urgent. The patient is a 68-year-old male admitted for CHF exacerbation.
exercises.hint: A 200-word clinical specification produces better handoffs than a 20-word instruction followed by 15 rounds of 'what about his creatinine?'
exercises.cr: 1) Specifies which clinical details to include (vitals, meds, labs) 2) Defines output format (SBAR or structured sections) 3) Mentions what to flag as urgent or pending 4) Is substantially more detailed than 'summarize this patient'

exercises.title: Specify the output
exercises.sc: A primary care physician receives a panel of lab results for a diabetic patient and asks the AI to "analyze these labs." The AI returns a wall of text mixing normal and abnormal values with no clear structure.
exercises.task: Write a prompt that specifies exactly what the output should look like. Define the structure: table of results with reference ranges? Flagged abnormals? Trend comparison with prior labs? Clinical significance summary?
exercises.hint: If you handed this output to a colleague covering your patients, would they immediately see what needs attention without reading every word?
exercises.cr: 1) Specifies output format explicitly (table, flags, sections) 2) Names specific lab values or panels to focus on 3) Requests comparison with reference ranges or prior results 4) Defines what 'clinically significant' means in this context

exercises.title: Audience and tone
exercises.sc:
A patient was just diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes. You need to communicate about this condition to three audiences:

1. The patient (clear, empathetic, no jargon)
2. The referring endocrinologist (clinical, detailed)
3. The insurance company (justification for treatment plan)
exercises.task: Write a prompt for ONE audience that explicitly controls tone, reading level, and emphasis. Make it clear who the reader is and what they need to understand or act on.
exercises.hint: The patient wants to know 'what does this mean for my life?' The endocrinologist wants HbA1c trends and comorbidities. The insurer wants ICD codes and medical necessity.
exercises.cr: 1) Clearly identifies target audience 2) Specifies appropriate tone and reading level 3) Defines what to emphasize vs. omit for that audience 4) Sets length expectations 5) Shows audience-aware medical communication

exercises.title: Setting constraints
exercises.sc: You're asking the AI to draft a treatment plan for a post-surgical knee replacement patient. Without constraints, the AI either produces a two-line stub or a sprawling document with speculative recommendations and off-label drug suggestions.
exercises.task: Write a prompt with explicit constraints: what NOT to include (no off-label recommendations, no specific dosages without physician review), required sections, formatting rules, and documentation standards.
exercises.hint: Telling the AI what to avoid is critical in healthcare. 'Do not recommend specific dosages' and 'flag items requiring physician sign-off' are safety constraints.
exercises.cr: 1) Sets specific length or section constraints 2) Includes 'do not' instructions (safety boundaries) 3) Lists required sections (goals, interventions, timeline) 4) Mentions documentation standards or compliance 5) Demonstrates negative constraints for patient safety

exercises.title: Role assignment
exercises.sc: A hospitalist wrote a discharge summary for a patient with multiple comorbidities. You want the AI to review it, but generic feedback misses clinical nuances.
exercises.task: Write a prompt that assigns the AI a specific clinical role (e.g., 'You are a board-certified internal medicine physician with 20 years of hospital medicine experience'). Define what expertise to apply and what to evaluate.
exercises.hint: A pharmacist catches medication interactions. A case manager catches missing follow-up appointments. A coding specialist catches documentation gaps. The role shapes the review.
exercises.cr: 1) Assigns a specific clinical role with credentials 2) Defines what expertise to apply 3) Specifies what to evaluate in the discharge summary 4) Role choice meaningfully shapes the clinical feedback

exercises.title: Iterative refinement
exercises.sc:
You asked the AI to write a discharge summary and got:

"Patient was admitted for pneumonia. Treatment was given. Patient improved and is being discharged with follow-up."

No specifics on the organism, antibiotic course, oxygen requirements, or what 'improved' means clinically.
exercises.task: Write a follow-up prompt that fixes this. Don't start over — refine. Tell the AI specifically what's missing and what clinical details to add.
exercises.hint: Good refinement is surgical: 'Add the antibiotic regimen with dates, O2 requirements on admission vs. discharge, and specific follow-up instructions including return precautions.' Bad: 'Make it more detailed.'
exercises.cr: 1) References specific problems in the original output 2) Gives targeted clinical corrections 3) Adds missing specifics (meds, vitals, timelines) 4) Shows refinement over restarting 5) Demonstrates iterative improvement cycle

exercises.title: Plan before you ask
exercises.sc:
Your department needs a new clinical protocol for managing sepsis in the ED. If you just say 'write a sepsis protocol,' you'll get a textbook summary that doesn't fit your facility's resources, staffing, or patient population.

The principle: spend 10 minutes planning the specification to avoid hours of revision.
exercises.task: Write a detailed specification prompt (150-250 words). Include: purpose, target clinicians, required protocol sections, evidence base, facility constraints, formatting, and exclusions.
exercises.hint: Your specification IS the prompt. Include details like 'community hospital, no 24/7 intensivist coverage, average ED volume 120 patients/day.'
exercises.cr: 1) Defines purpose and target clinicians 2) Lists specific protocol sections 3) References evidence-based guidelines (e.g., Surviving Sepsis Campaign) 4) Includes facility-specific constraints 5) Sets format and length 6) Spec itself is 100+ words

exercises.title: Chain-of-thought
exercises.sc: A 45-year-old woman presents with acute chest pain, dyspnea, and a heart rate of 112. She's on oral contraceptives and returned from a 14-hour flight two days ago. You need the AI to work through differential diagnosis systematically, not just jump to the most common answer.
exercises.task: Write a prompt forcing step-by-step clinical reasoning: first list differentials, then evaluate each against the presentation, then rank by probability, then recommend next diagnostic steps. Use explicit step numbering.
exercises.hint: Chain-of-thought: 'Before giving your assessment, first list all plausible differentials, then evaluate each against the history, risk factors, and vitals.' This prevents anchoring bias.
exercises.cr: 1) Uses explicit numbered steps 2) Separates differential generation from evaluation 3) Asks for clinical reasoning before conclusions 4) Includes risk factor analysis 5) Steps build logically toward a diagnostic plan

exercises.title: Few-shot examples
exercises.sc:
Your ED needs a triage system to categorize incoming patient complaints by acuity level: ESI-1 (Resuscitation), ESI-2 (Emergent), ESI-3 (Urgent), ESI-4 (Less Urgent), ESI-5 (Non-Urgent).

Examples:
- "Unresponsive, not breathing" -> ESI-1
- "Crushing chest pain, diaphoretic" -> ESI-2
- "Laceration with controlled bleeding, needs sutures" -> ESI-4
exercises.task: Write a prompt using few-shot examples that teaches the AI to triage new patient presentations. Include examples in consistent format, define all ESI levels, and add 2-3 test cases for the AI to categorize.
exercises.hint: Format consistency matters: if examples use '->' for mapping, use it for all. Cover each ESI level with at least one example.
exercises.cr: 1) Includes 3+ clear example pairs with ESI levels 2) Defines all 5 ESI categories 3) Examples cover multiple acuity levels 4) Includes new test cases 5) Consistent format throughout

exercises.title: Structured output
exercises.sc: You need the AI to generate a pre-operative assessment checklist for a 72-year-old patient scheduled for hip replacement. Instead of a narrative paragraph, you want a structured clinical form that the surgical team can actually use.
exercises.task: Write a prompt that enforces specific output structure. Define exact sections (patient demographics, comorbidities, medications, allergies, lab review, risk score, clearance status), what goes in each, and how to flag concerns.
exercises.hint: Show the exact format you want. A table with columns like 'Item | Status | Notes | Action Required' is more useful than prose.
exercises.cr: 1) Defines exact structure with sections or columns 2) Explains what goes in each section 3) Provides risk criteria or clearance logic 4) Handles edge cases (missing data, relative contraindications) 5) Optionally includes example row

exercises.title: Compare and evaluate
exercises.sc:
A patient with moderate COPD needs long-term maintenance therapy. Two options are on the table:

A: LABA/ICS combination (Fluticasone/Salmeterol)
B: LABA/LAMA combination (Umeclidinium/Vilanterol)

The attending wants a structured comparison before the care conference.
exercises.task: Write a prompt that evaluates both treatment options against specific clinical criteria and provides a recommendation. Define 3-4 criteria, ask for per-criterion scoring, and require evidence-based justification.
exercises.hint: Don't ask 'which is better?' Instead: 'Score each 1-5 on exacerbation reduction, side effect profile, patient adherence factors, and cost-effectiveness.'
exercises.cr: 1) Defines 3+ clinical criteria 2) Asks for per-criterion scores 3) Requires evidence-based reasoning 4) Requests justified recommendation considering patient factors 5) Meaningful non-overlapping criteria

exercises.title: Multi-step decomposition
exercises.sc:
A patient presents with unexplained weight loss, fatigue, and intermittent fevers over 3 months. The attending says: 'Work up this patient — full diagnostic workup with differentials, labs, imaging, and specialist referrals.'

Too complex for one prompt. Needs decomposition.
exercises.task: Write a SEQUENCE of 3-4 prompts that decompose this diagnostic workup. Each builds on the previous output. Show the full chain from history gathering through final assessment.
exercises.hint: Workflow: History/ROS analysis -> Differential generation -> Targeted lab/imaging plan -> Synthesis and referral recommendations. Each step has clear input and output.
exercises.cr: 1) Breaks into 3+ sequential prompts 2) Each has a focused clinical objective 3) Later prompts reference earlier outputs 4) Covers history -> differentials -> diagnostics -> synthesis 5) Demonstrates clinical decomposition

exercises.title: Error correction
exercises.sc:
The AI produced this clinical assessment:

"Patient has a cough and fever. Diagnosis: bronchitis. Plan: prescribe azithromycin 500mg x5 days."

Problems: skipped differential diagnosis, assumed bacterial etiology without evidence, no mention of vital signs or exam findings, didn't consider pneumonia or COVID, antibiotic may be unnecessary.
exercises.task: Write a prompt correcting these clinical reasoning errors. Ask for proper differential workup, evidence-based antibiotic stewardship, and complete documentation.
exercises.hint: Point out exactly what's wrong: 'You jumped to a bacterial diagnosis without considering viral etiology, didn't mention chest X-ray or oxygen saturation, and prescribed antibiotics without meeting prescribing criteria.'
exercises.cr: 1) Identifies specific clinical reasoning errors 2) Asks for proper differential diagnosis 3) Addresses antibiotic stewardship 4) Requests complete documentation 5) Shows critical clinical thinking

exercises.title: Persona prompting
exercises.sc:
A complex patient case needs multidisciplinary review: 58-year-old diabetic with a non-healing foot ulcer, recent cardiac stent, and depression. Stress-test the care plan from three perspectives:

1. Vascular surgeon (surgical viability, perfusion)
2. Clinical pharmacist (drug interactions, anticoagulation)
3. Wound care nurse (daily management, infection signs)
exercises.task: Write a prompt that has the AI adopt each clinical persona sequentially, critique the care plan, then synthesize into a unified multidisciplinary recommendation.
exercises.hint: Each persona surfaces different concerns. The surgeon asks about ankle-brachial index. The pharmacist flags dual antiplatelet + anticoagulant risk. The wound care nurse asks about offloading and dressing protocol.
exercises.cr: 1) Defines 3 distinct clinical personas 2) Each has specific clinical concerns 3) Sequential analysis from each perspective 4) Requests synthesis into unified plan 5) Shows how persona shapes clinical analysis

exercises.title: Prompt templates
exercises.sc: Every shift change, nurses do a bedside handoff for each patient. Instead of writing a new prompt each time, you want a reusable SBAR template that any nurse can fill in and get a structured handoff summary.
exercises.task: Create a reusable prompt template with [BRACKET] variables. Include: patient identifiers, situation, background, assessment, recommendation, pending items. Should work for any patient on any shift.
exercises.hint: Variables like [PATIENT_AGE_SEX], [PRIMARY_DIAGNOSIS], [CURRENT_VITALS], [ACTIVE_MEDS] make it reusable across every handoff.
exercises.cr: 1) Uses clear bracket variables 2) Genuinely reusable for any patient/shift 3) Covers SBAR framework completely 4) 4+ variable placeholders 5) Would save time every shift change

exercises.title: Patient chart review
exercises.sc: You're covering for a colleague and need to quickly review a complex patient's chart. Mrs. Delgado is a 74-year-old with CHF, CKD stage 3, atrial fibrillation, and Type 2 diabetes. She's been admitted for 6 days with multiple medication changes and two specialist consults.
exercises.task: Write a prompt producing a structured chart review: active problem list with status, medication reconciliation, recent lab trends, consultant recommendations, and outstanding action items.
exercises.hint: Structure your prompt like a clinical checklist: what to extract from each section of the chart, how to flag discrepancies, how to present it for rapid decision-making.
exercises.cr: 1) Lists clinical domains to review (problems, meds, labs, consults) 2) Defines how to assess status of each problem 3) Specifies structured output format 4) Includes mechanism for flagging discrepancies 5) Covers outstanding action items 6) Professional clinical output

exercises.title: Patient queue prioritization
exercises.sc: You're the charge nurse on a busy medical floor. 14 patients need attention this morning: new admissions, pending discharges, a patient whose blood pressure dropped overnight, medication reconciliations, and a family meeting. You need to triage your team's workload.
exercises.task: Write a prompt that prioritizes the patient queue by clinical urgency and required action. Define acuity categories, urgency criteria, and a scannable output format for the nursing team.
exercises.hint: Priority Matrix: Clinically unstable (immediate), Time-sensitive orders (within 1 hour), Routine care (scheduled), Administrative (when available).
exercises.cr: 1) Defines triage categories with clinical criteria 2) Specifies urgency levels 3) Distinguishes immediate/scheduled/deferrable actions 4) Scannable output format 5) Practical for real shift management

exercises.title: Clinical rounds notes
exercises.sc: Morning rounds covered 8 patients in 45 minutes. The attending discussed assessment changes, new orders, and disposition plans. Your scribbled notes are barely legible. Topics: Mr. Kim's worsening renal function, Mrs. Patel's discharge plan, the new sepsis admit in bed 4, and a goals-of-care discussion for Mr. Thompson.
exercises.task: Write a prompt transforming rough rounds notes into structured clinical documentation: per-patient sections with assessment, plan changes, new orders, and follow-up items with responsible providers.
exercises.hint: Template: Patient ID, Updated Assessment, Plan Changes, New Orders, Pending Items, Disposition, Responsible Provider.
exercises.cr: 1) Defines per-patient output sections 2) Action items have responsible provider + timeframe 3) Handles ambiguity in rough notes 4) Prioritizes assessment changes and new orders 5) Includes disposition status

exercises.title: Treatment cost comparison
exercises.sc:
A patient with moderate rheumatoid arthritis needs to choose between treatment options:
- Methotrexate (oral, weekly) + folic acid
- Adalimumab (Humira) biologic injection every 2 weeks
- Tofacitinib (Xeljanz) oral JAK inhibitor daily

Insurance covers 80% after deductible. The patient wants to understand total out-of-pocket costs over 12 months.
exercises.task: Write a prompt for a structured cost comparison: time horizon, all cost categories (drug, administration, monitoring labs, specialist visits), explicit assumptions, and a recommendation format that includes both cost and clinical factors.
exercises.hint: Include: drug cost, lab monitoring frequency, specialist visits, infusion center fees, patient assistance programs. State all assumptions about insurance and deductible.
exercises.cr: 1) All cost categories including monitoring and visits 2) Clear 12-month timeframe 3) Explicit assumptions about insurance coverage 4) Summary comparison table 5) Recommendation balancing cost and clinical effectiveness 6) Notes on patient assistance programs

exercises.title: Clinical research summary
exercises.sc: The department chief asks for a 5-page summary of recent evidence on early mobilization in ICU patients for the hospital's quality improvement committee. It needs to be data-driven, cite key studies, and include actionable recommendations for your 24-bed medical ICU.
exercises.task: Write the specification prompt — the detailed brief for a committee-ready clinical research summary on the first try. Structure, length per section, evidence requirements, tone, and exclusions.
exercises.hint: This is the ultimate 'plan before you ask' exercise. A 200-word specification with specific study types, outcome measures, and facility context produces a usable first draft.
exercises.cr: 1) Defines structure with specific sections 2) Length per section 3) Evidence requirements (RCTs, meta-analyses, guidelines) 4) Professional tone appropriate for QI committee 5) Exclusions (e.g., pediatric, surgical ICU) 6) Spec is 150+ words 7) Would produce committee-ready output

exercises.title: Breaking bad news
exercises.sc:
A 52-year-old patient's biopsy results confirm Stage IIIA non-small cell lung cancer. You need to prepare communication for:
1. The patient and spouse (empathetic, clear, hopeful but honest)
2. The referring physician (clinical details, staging, recommended next steps)
3. The tumor board presentation (structured case summary for multidisciplinary review)
exercises.task: Write one prompt producing all three communications with different tones but consistent clinical facts. Address the emotional weight of the patient communication while maintaining clinical precision for colleagues.
exercises.hint: Facts are identical across documents, framing changes dramatically. The patient needs to understand prognosis and next steps without being overwhelmed. The tumor board needs TNM staging and molecular markers.
exercises.cr: 1) Requests all three communications 2) Different tones appropriate to each audience 3) Consistent clinical facts across all three 4) Addresses emotional aspects of patient communication 5) Handles the sensitivity with appropriate frameworks (e.g., SPIKES) 6) Strategic clinical communication

exercises.title: Resident evaluation
exercises.sc: End-of-rotation evaluation for a PGY-2 internal medicine resident. You've observed them for 4 weeks across ICU, floor, and clinic settings. Need to assess clinical competency across ACGME milestones: patient care, medical knowledge, practice-based learning, interpersonal skills, professionalism, systems-based practice.
exercises.task: Write a prompt creating a systematic evaluation: scored criteria across ACGME competencies, specific behavioral examples, strengths/areas for growth, and actionable development recommendations.
exercises.hint: Chain-of-thought: observe behaviors -> map to competencies -> score against milestones -> identify patterns -> recommend development. Weighted scoring prevents recency bias.
exercises.cr: 1) Scored criteria across multiple ACGME competencies 2) Requires specific behavioral examples 3) Distinguishes strengths from growth areas 4) Comparison framework against milestone levels 5) Actionable development recommendations 6) Multiple evaluation techniques combined

exercises.title: Patient outcome analysis
exercises.sc:
Your department has 6 months of data on 150 heart failure readmissions. You need to:
1. Categorize readmission causes
2. Identify modifiable risk factors
3. Prioritize interventions
4. Report to the quality improvement committee

This is the capstone: combine every technique you've learned.
exercises.task: Write a comprehensive prompt for this end-to-end clinical analysis pipeline. Use few-shot for cause categorization, chain-of-thought for risk factor analysis, structured output for the QI report, and persona prompting for multidisciplinary review.
exercises.hint: Capstone: combine every technique. Few-shot for categorization + chain-of-thought for analysis + structured output for reporting + planning for the full pipeline.
exercises.cr: 1) Few-shot examples for readmission categorization 2) Clear clinical categories 3) Chain-of-thought risk factor identification 4) Prioritization criteria for interventions 5) Structured QI report output 6) 3+ techniques combined 7) Reusable clinical workflow

POST-SURGICAL CONTEXT

Patient: Dorothy Chen, 66F
Procedure: Right total knee arthroplasty (TKA), 03/26/2026
Surgeon: Dr. Alvarez, Orthopedics

Pre-op Conditions: Osteoarthritis (severe, right knee), HTN, Obesity (BMI 33), GERD
Allergies: Sulfa (rash), Codeine (nausea)

Current Status (POD 2):
- Pain: 5/10 at rest, 7/10 with PT (managed with multimodal protocol)
- ROM: 45 degrees flexion (goal: 90 by week 2)
- Weight-bearing: As tolerated with walker
- Wound: Clean, dry, intact. No erythema or drainage.
- Vitals: Stable, afebrile

Current Medications:
- Acetaminophen 1000mg q6h scheduled
- Oxycodone 5mg q4h PRN (using ~3x/day)
- Celecoxib 200mg BID
- Enoxaparin 40mg SQ daily (VTE prophylaxis, 14 days)
- Pantoprazole 40mg daily
- Lisinopril 20mg daily (home med)
- Ice and elevation protocol

PT Goals:
- POD 1-3: Transfer training, gait with walker, ROM exercises
- Week 1-2: Stair negotiation, increased ROM, reduced assistive device
- Week 3-6: Strengthening, balance, functional mobility
- Week 6-12: Return to full activity, discontinue assistive device

Discharge Criteria:
- Pain controlled on oral meds
- Independent transfers
- Demonstrate home exercise program
- Safe home environment confirmed

Compliance Notes:
- Document all PT sessions with objective measurements
- VTE prophylaxis per AAOS guidelines
- No NSAID use beyond 14 days post-op (renal risk with HTN)
- Follow-up: Surgeon 2 weeks, PCP 4 weeks

materials.7:
SEPSIS PROTOCOL CONTEXT

Facility: Riverside Community Hospital
- 180-bed community hospital
- ED volume: ~120 patients/day
- ICU: 12 beds, no 24/7 intensivist (hospitalist-managed with tele-ICU)
- Lab turnaround: 45-60 minutes for stat labs
- Blood culture turnaround: 48-72 hours
- Pharmacy: 24/7 on-site pharmacist

Current Gaps:
- Sepsis bundle compliance: 62% (target: 85%)
- Average time to antibiotics: 98 minutes (target: <60 minutes)
- Lactate recheck compliance: 48%
- No standardized screening tool in ED triage

Evidence Base:
- Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 Guidelines
- CMS SEP-1 Sepsis Core Measure
- Society of Critical Care Medicine recommendations

Required Protocol Sections:
- ED triage screening criteria
- Sepsis bundle (1-hour and 3-hour)
- Fluid resuscitation algorithm
- Vasopressor initiation criteria
- Lab ordering protocol (lactate, cultures, CBC, BMP, coags, procalcitonin)
- Escalation criteria (floor to ICU)
- Documentation requirements for CMS compliance
- Nursing and physician responsibilities by role

- Progressive dyspnea, now winded walking across room
- No cough, no hemoptysis, no fever
- Returned from business trip to Tokyo 2 days ago (14-hour flight)
- No prior episodes

Past Medical History:
- Migraine headaches
- Oral contraceptive use (combined estrogen/progesterone) x 8 years
- BMI: 28
- No prior surgeries
- No known clotting disorders

Family History:
- Mother: DVT at age 50
- Father: Hypertension, alive

- BP 128/82, HR 112, RR 22, O2 sat 93% on room air, Temp 99.1F

Physical Exam:
- Anxious, mildly diaphoretic
- Lungs: Clear bilaterally, no wheezing or rales
- Heart: Tachycardic, regular rhythm, no murmurs
- Legs: Mild left calf swelling, tender to palpation

COPD TREATMENT COMPARISON

Patient: Richard Gomez, 63M
Diagnosis: Moderate COPD (GOLD Stage II, Group B)
FEV1: 58% predicted | CAT Score: 18 | 1 exacerbation in past year
Comorbidities: HTN, BPH, former smoker (quit 2 years ago, 30 pack-year history)

OPTION A: LABA/ICS — Fluticasone/Salmeterol (Advair Diskus 250/50)
- Mechanism: Long-acting bronchodilator + inhaled corticosteroid
- Dosing: 1 inhalation BID
- Evidence: TORCH trial — reduced exacerbations by 25% vs placebo
- Side effects: Oral candidiasis (5-8%), hoarseness, possible pneumonia risk with ICS
- Cost: ~$380/month (brand), ~$45/month (generic fluticasone/salmeterol)
- Monitoring: Annual bone density if long-term ICS, oral hygiene

OPTION B: LABA/LAMA — Umeclidinium/Vilanterol (Anoro Ellipta)
- Mechanism: Dual bronchodilator (anticholinergic + beta-agonist)
- Dosing: 1 inhalation daily
- Evidence: FLAME trial — LABA/LAMA non-inferior to LABA/ICS for exacerbation prevention
- Side effects: Dry mouth (3%), urinary retention risk (caution with BPH), headache
- Cost: ~$420/month (no generic available)
- Monitoring: BPH symptoms, heart rate

- Group B: LABA/LAMA preferred over LABA/ICS unless eosinophils >300 or history of asthma
- ICS recommended if blood eosinophils >300 cells/mcL or frequent exacerbations

RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS TREATMENT OPTIONS

Patient: Patricia Novak, 52F
Diagnosis: Moderate RA (DAS28 score: 4.2, active disease)
Duration: 18 months since diagnosis

Comorbidities: Mild hepatic steatosis (NAFLD), HTN
Insurance: Aetna PPO, $2,000 deductible (met), 80/20 coinsurance, $6,500 OOP max

OPTION A — Methotrexate + Folic Acid (Continue + Optimize):
- Drug cost: ~$25/month (generic MTX 20mg/week) + $8/month (folic acid)
- Labs: CBC + CMP every 8 weeks ($45 per draw, insurance covers 80%)
- Rheumatology visits: Every 3 months ($75 copay)
- Rationale: May add sulfasalazine or hydroxychloroquine (triple therapy)
- Triple therapy drug cost: ~$80/month total
- Risks: Hepatotoxicity (concern with NAFLD), GI side effects

OPTION B — Adalimumab (Humira) Biologic:
- Drug cost: ~$6,800/month (list price), biosimilar ~$3,400/month
- Patient cost: 20% coinsurance = ~$680-1,360/month until OOP max
- Humira patient assistance: Co-pay card reduces to ~$5/month (if eligible)
- Administration: Self-injection every 2 weeks
- Labs: TB test before starting, CBC + CMP every 3 months ($45/draw)
- Rheumatology visits: Every 3 months ($75 copay)
- Risks: Infection risk (screen for TB, Hep B), injection site reactions
- Monitoring: Annual TB screening, watch for signs of infection

OPTION C — Tofacitinib (Xeljanz) JAK Inhibitor:
- Drug cost: ~$5,200/month (brand only)
- Patient cost: 20% coinsurance = ~$1,040/month until OOP max
- Pfizer co-pay program: May reduce to $0 for eligible commercially insured
- Administration: Oral tablet, 5mg BID
